# Changes in utilization of online pediatric educational resources during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic

**Authors:** Dennis Daniel; Anna Krotinger; Traci Wolbrink

**Affiliations:** 1 Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2 Department of Anesthesiology, Critical Care, and Pain Medicine, Boston Children's Hospital, Boston, Massachusetts, USA

## Abstract

The COVID‐19 global pandemic disrupted healthcare, society, and medical education. Use of online video educational content increased at the onset of the COVID‐19 pandemic, across two platforms. This demonstrates the potential of online videos to provide timely information in a scalable fashion, quickly meeting clinical information needs.

The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2) viral pandemic disrupted healthcare and society worldwide in unprecedented ways, with social distancing guidelines interrupting in‐person work and education, threatening the ability of trainees and independently practicing clinicians to develop the essential knowledge to care for patients safely and effectively. 1 , 2 Furthermore, illness and quarantine of medical personnel, and the sheer number of patients requiring care, have contributed to shortages of trained and experienced staff to care for seriously ill patients. 3 , 4 Given these challenges, it is essential for clinical knowledge, both relating specifically to the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) as well as to the care of critically ill patients in general, to be readily accessible. A wide range of Internet‐based learning resources (websites, material distributed via third‐party platforms, etc.) and communication technologies (videoconferencing, discussion boards, chat, and email) are available to promote larger‐scale knowledge exchange. 5 The shifting of educational strategies, with increased reliance on Web‐based learning resources and videoconferencing solutions during the COVID‐19 pandemic, has been described by other authors. 6 , 7

Although it is reasonable to assume that engagement with e‐learning platforms and resources would increase due to the COVID‐19 pandemic, there are limited published data available that quantify the usage of individual e‐learning platforms during this period, or the extent to which changes in these utilization rates may be associated with accessing COVID‐19 related content. 8 This large‐scale disruptive medical event provides an opportunity to quantitatively test the assumption that engagement with online resources increases as part of the effort to optimize educational practices. To this end, we examined the utilization of a set of video resources made available by OPENPediatrics, an open‐access e‐learning initiative targeted at pediatric clinicians, that provides access to materials freely via their dedicated Web platform (http://www.openpediatrics.org), as well as through public third‐party content distribution platforms such as YouTube.

For the period of November 2019 through July 2020, we examined pageview data from the OPENPediatrics.org website gathered via the Google Analytics web‐based service (Google, LLC, Mountain View, California, USA), as well as from the OPENPediatrics YouTube channel (via YouTube Studio, also owned by Google). We selected this time period in order to include data from at least two months before the first announcement of a cluster of viral pneumonia. 9 We ended the included time interval in July 2020 in order to avoid the introduction of technical confounders associated with the OPENPediatrics.org website migrating to a new learning management system in August 2020. We identified a set of videos that were available as of July 2020, and that had at least one view on both the OPENPediatrics website and the YouTube channel during this time period. For each video in this set, we used Google Analytics and YouTube Studio data to generate weekly counts of pageviews on OPENPediatrics.org and video views on the OPENPediatrics YouTube channel. Totals of weekly pageviews and video views were batched into three groupings of 13 consecutive weeks each (group 1, November 1, 2019 through January 30, 2020; group 2, January 31, 2020 through April 30, 2020; group 3, May 1, 2020 through July 31, 2020). Pageviews and video views by the group were respectively compared with one‐way ANOVA (with a pre‐determined significance threshold of P < 0.05) followed by post‐hoc two‐tailed t‐tests (with a pre‐determined significance threshold of P < 0.017, Bonferroni corrected for multiple testing).

In order to examine whether changes in use across the three groups were driven by users preferentially accessing content potentially more relevant to the care of patients with COVID‐19, we classified a subset of the included videos as “COVID‐relevant” (being primarily focused on evaluation and management of respiratory illnesses and/or shock states, addressing important ethical and other considerations in the care of seriously ill children, or teaching common inpatient and intensive care unit procedures). The authors first independently classified each content item as either COVID‐relevant or not, and then reconciled differences to arrive at a complete consensus. We focused on videos as opposed to other types of OPENPediatrics content (courses, simulators, documents, calculators, etc.) to facilitate direct comparison across the two platforms. Weekly counts of OPENPediatrics.org pageviews and YouTube video views were generated separately for the COVID‐relevant subset and the remainder of the overall set. A two‐way ANOVA was conducted on OPENPediatrics.org pageviews and YouTube video views respectively, with COVID‐relevance (yes or no) and group (group 1, group 2, and group 3) as factors. A pre‐determined significance threshold of P < 0.05 was established. Data were analyzed using Microsoft Excel (Microsoft Inc., Redmond, Washington, USA).

Tables S1 and S2 described the overall demographic characteristics of registered users on OPENPediatrics.org during the study period. A total of 552 videos were included for analysis across the two platforms. One hundred and seventy‐two of these videos (31.1%) were classified as COVID‐relevant. Overall during the 39‐week study period, there were 156 785 pageviews on OPENPediatrics.org and 3 832 077 video views on YouTube.com for the full video set. Of these, 78 188 site views (49.9%) and 2 144 381 video views (56.0%) were attributable to the COVID‐relevant video subset. Figure S1 displays the weekly view total for the website and YouTube, respectively, while Figure 1 displays the comparison of weekly views between the COVID‐relevant subset and the remainder of the videos.

*FIGURE 1: Views over time for coronavirus disease (COVID)‐relevant versus other videos. (A) Weekly video pageviews on OPENPediatrics.org. (B) Weekly video views on the OPENPediatrics YouTube channel.*

When examining one‐way ANOVA across the three groups, the date range had a significant impact on both the website pageviews (F = 10.150, P < 0.001) and YouTube video views (F = 8.728, P < 0.001). For website views, post‐hoc t‐tests demonstrated a statistically significant difference between groups 1 and 2 (average weekly views, 2695 vs. 4872, P = 0.003), and between groups 1 and 3 (2695 vs. 4493, P < 0.001), but not between groups 2 and 3 (4872 vs. 4493, P = 0.539). For YouTube views, post‐hoc t‐tests demonstrated a statistically significant difference between groups 1 and 2 (average weekly views, 87 548 vs. 111 491, P < 0.001), but not between groups 1 and 3 (87 548 vs. 95 736, P = 0.223) or group 2 and 3 (111 491 vs. 95 736, P = 0.033).

For the website views two‐way ANOVA, date range had a significant impact on average weekly views (F = 15.286, P < 0.001), with average weekly view count being higher for group 2 (mean weekly views = 2436) and group 3 (2247) as compared to group 1 (1347). However, a significant effect on COVID‐relevance was not found (F = 0.004, P = 0.952). The interaction between COVID‐relevance and the group was also not significant (F = 0.886, P = 0.417).

For the YouTube views two‐way ANOVA, date range also had a significant impact on average weekly views (F = 9.484, P < 0.001) with the average weekly view count again being higher for group 2 (mean weekly views = 55 746) and batch 3 (47 868) as compared to group 1 (43 773). A significant effect was also found for COVID‐relevance (F = 26.34, P < 0.001), as well as for the interaction between the group and COVID‐relevance (F = 4.294, P = 0.017). When examining the means, although the average weekly YouTube view count increased from group 1 to group 2 for both COVID‐relevant and other videos, the weekly view average for COVID‐relevant content in group 3 (56 701) stayed higher than group 1 (44 960), whereas the group 3 weekly view average for the content not designated COVID‐relevant (39 034) dropped below the group 1 weekly average (42 587) (Table S3).

In this study, we found that overall utilization of OPENPediatrics video resources on both the clinician website and on YouTube increased from February 2020 onward as compared to the period of November through January 2020 and that this was still present, though not further significantly different, from May through July 2020. Overall, our findings provide quantitative support for the assertion that usage of online medical e‐learning resources significantly increased during the first year of the COVID‐19 pandemic. Interestingly, although the increased utilization appeared to be significantly driven by COVID‐relevant content on YouTube, with a transient boost to other OPENPediatrics content on that platform as well, the same effect of COVID‐relevance did not hold for the OPENPediatrics website. The difference in utilization patterns between the two platforms may be explained by factors including differences in the demographics of the respective user bases (for example, OPENPediatrics.org targets pediatric healthcare professionals and institutions providing health professions education, while YouTube is widely used by both pediatric and adult healthcare professionals, as well as laypeople); user motivations for seeking information on different websites; differences in how content is presented on each site; presence or absence of advertisements; the disproportionate impact of COVID on adults as opposed to children; differing levels of trust in the validity of the content on each respective platform; as well as other unmeasured factors.

Previously published research has asserted the importance of virtual and asynchronous approaches when an in‐person gathering is not possible, such as during widespread infectious pandemics, 10 where social distancing is implemented as a preventative measure to “flatten the curve” (in other words, to slow the spread of infection to reduce the risk of overwhelming healthcare resources) before more definitive therapies or vaccines are available. 11 , 12 Outside of the COVID‐19 pandemic, overall integration of e‐learning into healthcare professional education continues apace, 13 although barriers to implementation persist. 14 The current pandemic has obligated greater uptake and implementation of virtual learning strategies, but the extent to which the current changes to the medical educational environment will be sustained is unclear at this time. 15 It is reasonable to expect that some learning objectives will be achieved through virtual approaches, while many elements of healthcare professional education will continue to obligate in‐person interaction. 16 In any case, although there are numerous perspectives and approaches to healthcare education in general, let alone in the context of a pandemic, data‐driven approaches to characterizing the behaviors of medical learners in online spaces remain poorly represented in the educational literature.

Our study has a number of limitations. Due to the limitations of our datasets, we were unable to subdivide utilization data by country or world region, nor were we able to examine other metrics of engagement data such as time spent using particular resources. We only reviewed engagement data pertaining to videos produced by the OPENPediatrics program, and there is a wide range of other forms of content made available by OPENPediatrics on the website, as well as more generally available for consumption on the Internet; it is unclear if user engagement with these other types of educational content will follow similar patterns to those described herein. Our classification scheme for determining COVID‐relevant content was pragmatic and is not validated across other sets of educational content. Although we appreciated a clear signal of increased engagement with this overall body of material in temporal association with the COVID‐19 pandemic, as well as evidence supporting specific interest in what we have defined as COVID‐relevant material, the question of whether the engagement behaviors described here generalize to other e‐learning platforms requires further research. The OPENPediatrics platform is focused on knowledge exchange pertaining to the care of sick children, whereas the COVID‐19 pandemic has taken its greatest toll on individuals of adult age; therefore, the engagement patterns depicted here may underestimate the overall interest in COVID‐relevant material driven by this disruptive medical event. Finally, our data only permitted us to measure general trends in resource access; specific questions about clinician motivations for seeking specific online learning materials were beyond the scope of this study.

Overall, we have quantitatively demonstrated increased utilization of online pediatric educational resources across two platforms during the early days of the COVID‐19 pandemic and highlighted differences in use patterns over time and between different types of e‐learning platforms. We hope these findings will reinforce the importance of making high‐quality medical educational content widely available during globally disruptive medical events. Future investigation should examine the dynamics and motivators of learner engagement in the online domain in greater detail.

This retrospective analysis of anonymous and aggregated website engagement data was determined to be exempt from review by the Institutional Review Board at Boston Children’s Hospital.
